parts.context: The owner of a small tutoring business and her coordinator are dealing with a staffing problem.

lines: Dev, you might want to sit down for this. Anton just quit.
Quit? As in, he’s not coming in tomorrow?
As in, he’s not coming in at all. He got a full-time offer from an engineering firm in Calgary, and they want him to start on Monday. He apologized about five times, but that doesn’t really help us.
Two weeks before exams. That’s the worst possible timing. How many students does he have booked?
Fourteen. Nine for Grade Twelve physics and five for calculus. Most of them bought the exam prep package, so they’ve already paid for six sessions each.
And the parents of those kids are exactly the ones who’ll be furious. Some of them chose us specifically because of Anton. Mrs. Ochoa told me her son’s physics mark went up fifteen points with him.

I know. And honestly, I’m less worried about losing the money than losing the reputation. If we let fourteen families down in January, word will get around every high school in the district by February.
Could you take some of them yourself? You taught physics for years.

In theory, yes. But I’m already at thirty hours a week with my own students, and I’m doing all the admin for the new location. If I add fourteen more students, something’s going to slip, and it’ll probably be the quality of my teaching.
Okay. So we need another tutor, and fast.
Fast, and good. Parents who are paying for exam prep will notice very quickly if the new person doesn’t know the material inside out.

qs.q: Why did Anton leave?
o: He was unhappy with the new exam prep package.
He moved to Calgary to continue his own studies.
He had a serious disagreement with several parents.
He took a permanent job with a company elsewhere.
qs.ev: He got a full-time offer from an engineering firm in Calgary
qs.x: A full-time offer from an engineering firm is a permanent job, not further studies. No conflict with parents is mentioned; the parents actually liked him.

qs.q: What is Marguerite most concerned about?
o: Refunding the money that parents have already paid
Harm to the business’s standing in the community
Finding another physics tutor before Monday
Mrs. Ochoa’s son doing poorly on his exam
qs.ev: I’m less worried about losing the money than losing the reputation
qs.x: She says the reputation matters more than the money, since news would spread to every school. Refunds are the smaller worry, so option A reverses her priority.

qs.q: Why does Marguerite hesitate to take on Anton’s students herself?
o: She has never taught physics at the Grade Twelve level.
She is planning to move to the new location soon.
Her heavy workload could lower the standard of her lessons.
The parents have specifically asked for Anton.
qs.ev: something’s going to slip, and it’ll probably be the quality of my teaching
qs.x: She already works thirty hours plus admin, so more students would hurt quality. Dev says she taught physics for years, and the new location adds admin, not a move.

lines: What about posting on the university job board? There are always grad students looking for extra money, and a physics grad student would be perfect.

I thought about that. The problem is the police check. Our policy is that every tutor working with minors has a vulnerable sector check, and in this city it’s taking about three weeks. By the time it clears, the exams are over.
Could we make an exception, just this once? Maybe if a parent is always in the room?
No. That policy is the one thing I’m not willing to bend. If anything ever went wrong, we’d have no defence, and frankly, I’d never forgive myself.
Fair enough. What about referring them to Apex Learning? They have physics tutors.
Apex is our main competitor. If we send fourteen families there, how many do you think come back next year?
Right. Probably none. Okay, here’s another thought. Shirin already has her check, and she’s strong in calculus. She told me last week she wanted more hours.
Shirin could take the five calculus students, absolutely. But she’s said herself that she isn’t comfortable with physics past Grade Eleven. I wouldn’t ask her to fake it.
So that covers calculus but still leaves nine physics students.
Nine students, all preparing for the same exam, all covering the same units.
Are you thinking what I’m thinking? Group sessions?

qs.q: Why can they not hire a graduate student from the job board?
o: A required background check would not be ready in time.
Graduate students charge more than the business can pay.
The university does not let its students tutor privately.
Parents prefer tutors who have classroom experience.
qs.ev: in this city it’s taking about three weeks
qs.x: The police check takes about three weeks, which is after the exams. Money and university rules are never raised; grad students would actually be “perfect”.

qs.q: How does Marguerite respond to Dev’s idea of making an exception?
o: She agrees, as long as a parent stays in the room.
She says she will ask the families before deciding.
She is willing to bend the policy just this once.
She will not compromise on this particular rule.
qs.ev: That policy is the one thing I’m not willing to bend.
qs.x: Her immediate “No” and “not willing to bend” show a firm refusal. Having a parent in the room was Dev’s suggestion, which she rejects.

qs.q: Why does Marguerite reject referring students to Apex Learning?
o: Apex’s tutors are less qualified than her own.
Apex has no spaces available before the exams.
The families would probably stay with Apex afterward.
Apex would charge the families much higher fees.
qs.ev: how many do you think come back next year?
qs.x: Her question implies families sent to a competitor would not return, and Dev answers “Probably none.” Apex does have physics tutors, so availability is not the issue.

lines: Exactly. If I run three group sessions for the physics students, two-hour reviews on the next three Saturdays, I can cover all nine without adding much to my week. And they’re writing the same exam, so the content is identical.
Parents paid for one-on-one, though. Won’t they feel short-changed?
That’s why we’ll offer two choices. They can switch to the group sessions with a partial refund, since group time costs us less, or they can take a full refund. No pressure either way.
How much of a refund for the group option?
Their package was four hundred and twenty dollars. Let’s refund half. Two-ten.
That’s generous. I think most of them will take it.
I’d rather be generous now than defensive later. Can you draft the email to the parents tonight? I want it out by noon tomorrow, before any of them hear about Anton from their kids.
Sure. Should I mention why he left?

Just say he’s accepted a full-time position and wishes the students well. Keep it short. And call Shirin first thing tomorrow to confirm the calculus students before the email goes out. I don’t want to promise something we can’t deliver.
Will do. I’ll send you the draft by nine tonight, and I’ll call Shirin at eight tomorrow.
Perfect. And Dev, thank you. This would have been a much worse day without you.

qs.q: How much would a parent who chooses the group option get back?
o: Nothing
qs.ev: Let’s refund half. Two-ten.
qs.x: The package cost $420 and half is refunded, so $210. A full $420 refund is the other choice, for families who do not want group sessions.

qs.q: Why does Marguerite want the email to go out quickly?
o: So that families hear the news from the business first
So that Shirin can begin teaching on Monday
So that parents can decide before Apex contacts them
So that refunds are processed before the exams
qs.ev: before any of them hear about Anton from their kids
qs.x: She wants parents to learn the news from the business, not from their children. Shirin will be called before the email, but her start date is not the reason for speed.

parts.context: An international high school student is talking with her homestay host.

lines: Luciana, have you got a minute? I wanted to talk about last night.
Is this about the time I came home? I’m really sorry. I tried to be quiet.

You were quiet, don’t worry. That’s not the issue. It was ten past one, and it’s the second time this week. Your agency’s rule is eleven on school nights for students under eighteen, and I’m responsible for you while you’re here.
I know. I wasn’t at a party, I promise. My chemistry study group meets at Daniela’s house, and we lost track of time. Then the bus I needed didn’t come for forty minutes.

I believe you. But put yourself in my shoes. At midnight, I had no idea where you were, and your phone went straight to voicemail. I was about ten minutes away from calling the agency’s emergency line.
My battery died. I should have borrowed Daniela’s phone. That was stupid of me.

Not stupid, just something to fix. Here’s what I’d suggest. If you’re going to be later than nine, send me a text with the address. And if it’s after ten and the buses are bad, call me. I’d much rather drive across town than lie awake wondering.
Honestly, I’d mind a lot less than another night like last night.
Okay. Thank you. Can I ask about something else while we’re talking? On weekends, I’d love to cook some Brazilian food. I miss my mother’s cooking. Would that be okay?
Of course. Use whatever you need. The only thing I’d ask is that you clean up the same evening. My wife starts work at six, and she likes the kitchen clear in the morning.
That’s fair. And one more thing. Daniela asked if she could sleep over on Saturday, after our study session.

Ah, that one I can’t decide on my own. The agency has a policy about overnight guests, and I believe they need to approve it in advance. Why don’t you email your coordinator tonight? If she says yes, it’s fine with us.
I’ll do that. And from now on, I’ll charge my phone before I leave.

qs.q: Why does Mr. Gallagher want to speak with Luciana?
o: She made too much noise when she came home late.
She missed a meeting with her agency coordinator.
She has broken a rule about returning home at night.
She has been skipping her chemistry study group.
qs.ev: Your agency’s rule is eleven on school nights for students under eighteen
qs.x: She came home after one, twice, breaking the eleven o’clock rule. He says explicitly that noise was not the issue.

qs.q: Why was Luciana late?
o: A long study session ran over and transport was slow.
She went to a party at Daniela’s house after class.
Her phone died, so she could not call for a taxi.
She took the wrong bus and ended up across town.
qs.ev: and we lost track of time
qs.x: The study group ran late and the bus took forty minutes. Her dead phone explains why she could not be reached, not why she was late.

qs.q: What does Mr. Gallagher suggest about the previous night?
o: He was angry that Luciana had lied to him.
He had already called the agency’s emergency line.
He suspected that Luciana had been at a party.
He had been very worried about her safety.
qs.ev: I was about ten minutes away from calling the agency’s emergency line
qs.x: Not knowing where she was and nearly calling the emergency line show serious worry. He was close to calling but did not, and he says he believes her.

qs.q: What does Mr. Gallagher offer to do?
o: Lend Luciana a phone charger for her trips
Drive her home if buses are a problem late
Extend her curfew to midnight on weekends
Speak to Daniela’s parents about the group
qs.ev: I’d much rather drive across town than lie awake wondering
qs.x: If it is after ten and the buses are bad, she should call and he will drive. He asks her to text, but he does not change the curfew.

qs.q: What will Luciana most likely do about Daniela’s sleepover?
o: Tell Daniela that sleepovers are not allowed
Ask Mr. Gallagher’s wife for permission
Request approval from the agency first
Invite Daniela only for dinner instead
qs.ev: Why don’t you email your coordinator tonight?
qs.x: The agency must approve overnight guests, so she will email her coordinator, and she agrees to. Sleepovers are not banned; they need approval.

parts.context: A working adult calls a college to ask about a part-time certificate program.

lines: Hello, I’m interested in the Human Resources certificate in your evening program. I work full-time, so I wanted to understand how it works before I apply.

Of course. The certificate is six courses. Most people take one course per term, so it takes two years, but if you take two courses in some terms, you can finish in about a year and a half. Classes run one evening a week, from six thirty to nine thirty, or you can take most courses online.
Right. Everything is available online except the final course, the Workplace Investigations capstone. That one includes role-plays, so it’s in person only, over six Saturdays.
Okay, I can manage Saturdays. Is there a particular order?
Just one rule. HR Foundations must be your first course. After that, you can take the rest in any order.

Each course is six hundred and eighty-nine dollars, plus a one-time program fee of a hundred and twenty. Many employers reimburse tuition, so keep your receipts. We issue an official tax receipt every February.
Here’s what I really wanted to ask. I’ve worked as an office manager for eight years, and I’ve done a lot of hiring and payroll. Do I really have to take every course?

Possibly not. We have something called recognition of prior learning. You put together a portfolio showing that you’ve already mastered a course’s content, with examples from your work, and an instructor assesses it. If it’s approved, you get the credit without taking the course.
That sounds perfect. How much is that?
Two hundred and fifty per course assessed, whether or not it’s approved. You can use it for a maximum of two courses in the certificate, and not for Foundations or the capstone.
So realistically, payroll and recruitment are the two I’d try.

That’s what most people in your position do. One tip, though: don’t submit a portfolio until you’ve finished Foundations. The instructors expect you to use the terms and frameworks taught there, and portfolios from people who skip ahead are often turned down.
Good to know. When does the next term start?
January twelfth. Registration officially closes on the fifth, but the online sections of Foundations usually fill by mid-December.
And if I register and then my work schedule changes?
You can withdraw for a full refund until the second class. After that, there’s no refund, but you can transfer once to a later term for a fifty-dollar fee.

qs.q: What is true about the format of the certificate?
o: All six courses can be completed entirely online.
Every course but one can be taken online.
The capstone course meets one evening a week.
Online courses may only be taken after the capstone.
qs.ev: Everything is available online except the final course
qs.x: Only the capstone is in person, so five of six courses can be online. The capstone meets on Saturdays, not weekday evenings.

qs.q: If Agnieszka takes all six courses, what will she pay in total for tuition and program fees?
qs.ev: plus a one-time program fee of a hundred and twenty
qs.x: Six courses at $689 cost $4,134, plus the one-time $120 fee, for $4,254. Option A forgets the program fee.

qs.q: What must Agnieszka do before her other courses?
o: Complete HR Foundations
Finish the Saturday capstone
Submit a work portfolio
Get her employer’s approval
qs.ev: HR Foundations must be your first course
qs.x: Foundations must come first; after that the order is free. The capstone is the final course, not the first.

qs.q: What is one limit on recognition of prior learning?
o: It is free if the portfolio is approved.
It can only be used for the capstone course.
It can replace no more than two courses.
It requires eight years of work experience.
qs.ev: You can use it for a maximum of two courses in the certificate
qs.x: It applies to at most two courses. It costs $250 whether or not it is approved, and it cannot be used for the capstone.

qs.q: Why does the adviser recommend waiting before submitting a portfolio?
o: Portfolios are assessed only once a year.
Assessors look for ideas taught in the first course.
Portfolio fees will go down after January.
The relevant courses are not offered until later.
qs.ev: The instructors expect you to use the terms and frameworks taught there
qs.x: Assessors expect the vocabulary and frameworks from Foundations, so portfolios submitted early are often rejected. Fees and timing of courses are not mentioned.

qs.q: What does the adviser imply about registering for January?
o: She should register well before the official deadline.
Online registration closes on the fifth of December.
In-person sections fill up faster than online ones.
Late registration is possible for a fifty-dollar fee.
qs.ev: the online sections of Foundations usually fill by mid-December
qs.x: Registration closes on January 5, but online sections fill by mid-December, so she should register early. The $50 fee is for transferring terms, not late registration.

parts.context: You will hear a news report about a new student residence.

lines: A downtown hotel that sat half-empty for three years will soon be home to more than three hundred students. Ridgeline College announced today that it has signed a ten-year lease on the former Parkside Inn, which will be converted into student residence rooms in time for the fall term. Each room will have a private bathroom and a small fridge, but there will be no individual kitchens. Instead, the hotel’s ground-floor restaurant will become a dining hall, and the former conference rooms will be turned into study spaces. Rent will be eight hundred and seventy-five dollars a month, roughly a third less than the average one-bedroom apartment in the city, but residents will be required to sign up for at least a ten-meal-a-week plan. The college says priority will go to first-year students from outside the region, followed by international students. Emeka Obi, a second-year nursing student, spent the first two months of last term sleeping on a friend’s sofa.

I applied to forty-something listings. Half didn’t answer, and the rest wanted a guarantor or six months’ rent up front. I was commuting from my friend’s place an hour and a half each way, and my grades really suffered. Honestly, if this had existed last year, I wouldn’t have thought twice. But I’ll say this: hotel rooms aren’t designed for long-term living. You need somewhere to cook, somewhere to put your stuff. I hope they’ve thought about that.

Neighbourhood groups have raised concerns of their own. The Parkside Inn is surrounded by family homes, and some residents worry about late-night noise. The college says it will hire residence staff to live on-site and enforce quiet hours from eleven p.m. City councillors, meanwhile, say the conversion is a short-term fix. The college’s own figures show it needs about twelve hundred more beds to meet demand, and the hotel covers barely a quarter of that. A new purpose-built residence is planned, but construction isn’t expected to begin for at least two years.

qs.q: What will the converted hotel rooms provide?
o: Private washrooms but no personal kitchens
Shared kitchens on each residential floor
A bedroom with a small kitchenette
Study spaces inside every room
qs.ev: there will be no individual kitchens
qs.x: Rooms have private bathrooms and fridges but no kitchens; meals come from the dining hall. Study spaces are in the former conference rooms, not in each room.

qs.q: Which condition applies to students who live there?
o: They must be in their first year of study.
They must provide a guarantor or six months’ rent.
They must pay for a plan covering some of their meals.
They must sign a lease for the full ten years.
qs.ev: residents will be required to sign up for at least a ten-meal-a-week plan
qs.x: A meal plan of at least ten meals a week is required. First-years get priority but are not the only ones allowed; the guarantor was a private landlord’s demand.

qs.q: How does Emeka feel about the hotel residence?
o: He is sure it will solve the city’s housing problem.
He welcomes it but doubts it suits long-term living.
He thinks it is too expensive for most students.
He believes the neighbours’ concerns are exaggerated.
qs.ev: hotel rooms aren’t designed for long-term living
qs.x: He says he would have taken it without hesitation but adds “But I’ll say this”, raising concerns about cooking and storage. He does not comment on cost or neighbours.

qs.q: What does Emeka say about his housing search last year?
o: Most landlords offered rooms he could not afford.
He found a place an hour and a half from campus.
The college guaranteed him a room after two months.
Landlords ignored him or set conditions he couldn’t meet.
qs.ev: Half didn’t answer, and the rest wanted a guarantor or six months’ rent up front
qs.x: Half did not reply and the rest demanded a guarantor or six months’ rent. The ninety-minute commute was from a friend’s sofa, not a place he found.

qs.q: What point do city councillors make?
o: The hotel will meet only a small part of the need.
The college should build a new residence immediately.
Residence staff will not be able to control noise.
The rent will be too high for most first-year students.
qs.ev: the hotel covers barely a quarter of that
qs.x: About 300 beds is barely a quarter of the 1,200 needed, so it is a short-term fix. Noise is the neighbours’ concern, not the councillors’.

parts.context: Three Grade Nine teachers are trying to agree on a policy for late assignments.

lines: Okay, the principal wants a common late-work policy for the whole Grade Nine team by the end of the month, so let’s try to get there today. Right now, I’m taking ten percent off per day, Farah has no penalty at all, and Josefina is somewhere in between. Parents have noticed, and frankly, so have the students.

I’ll start, since I’m the outlier. A mark is supposed to tell us what a student knows. If a student writes an excellent lab report three days late, docking thirty percent says she understands the science less well than she does. That’s just inaccurate.
But meeting deadlines is a skill too, Farah. Employers don’t accept reports a week late with no consequences. If we don’t teach that now, when do we?

I hear both of you, but I think we’re arguing about the wrong thing. In my class, the kids who hand things in late aren’t usually lazy. They’re the ones working weekend shifts, or looking after younger siblings, or the ones who froze because they didn’t know how to start.
Some of them, sure. But some are absolutely gaming the system. I had a student last term who handed in every assignment a week late because he knew he’d get extra time to see what his friends wrote.
And the penalty didn’t stop him, did it?

Here’s what I’ve been trying. Students get a forty-eight-hour grace period, no questions asked, but they have to fill out a short form saying when they’ll submit and what’s getting in the way. Most never need it. And the form tells me which kids need help with planning.
I like that a lot. It treats them like people, not suspects.
Right now, I take five percent a day, up to a maximum of twenty. So no assignment ever loses more than twenty percent.
Twenty percent maximum? Then my student would just hand everything in a week late and accept the twenty.

That’s why I’d add one more piece. Work isn’t accepted after the unit test. Once we’ve moved on, the window closes, and the assignment is recorded as incomplete. It’s the hard deadline that stops the gaming.
Hmm. A real final deadline. I could live with that. I’ve never actually wanted to give zeros; I just want deadlines to mean something.

I’m less comfortable with any penalty at all, to be honest. But I’ll accept five percent a day if students with an accommodation plan are exempt. Some of my students have extra time written into their plans, and a penalty would directly contradict that.
That’s non-negotiable anyway. Those plans are formal documents.
Agreed. So: a forty-eight-hour grace period with a form, then five percent a day up to twenty, nothing accepted after the unit test, and accommodation plans override all of it.
Can we call it a pilot? One term, and then we look at the data. If late submissions go up, I’ll admit I was wrong.
And if they go down, I’ll admit I was wrong. Deal. I’ll write it up for the principal by Friday.
I’ll make the form. Something short, so nobody can complain it’s more work than the assignment.

qs.q: Why does Hollis want the team to agree on a policy today?
o: The principal has complained about his ten percent penalty.
Students have asked the team for longer deadlines.
Farah’s approach has caused complaints from parents.
Differences between their approaches have become obvious.
qs.ev: Parents have noticed, and frankly, so have the students.
qs.x: The three teachers use very different rules, and parents and students have noticed. No one has complained about one teacher in particular.

qs.q: What is Farah’s main argument against late penalties?
o: They punish students who work weekend shifts.
They make a mark a less accurate picture of learning.
They encourage students to copy their friends’ work.
They contradict students’ formal accommodation plans.
qs.ev: That’s just inaccurate.
qs.x: She argues a penalty makes the mark misrepresent what a student knows. Weekend shifts are Josefina’s point, and accommodation plans come up only later as a condition.

qs.q: What does Josefina suggest about students who submit work late?
o: Most of them are trying to take advantage of the system.
They usually need a stricter penalty before they change.
Their lateness often has causes other than laziness.
They tend to be strong students who are perfectionists.
qs.ev: They’re the ones working weekend shifts, or looking after younger siblings
qs.x: She lists jobs, family duties and not knowing how to start, so lateness is rarely laziness. Gaming the system is Hollis’s view of some students.

qs.q: What does Hollis admit about his former student?
o: The penalty did not change the student’s behaviour.
The student had a good reason for being late.
The student eventually started submitting on time.
The student was caught copying his friends’ work.
qs.ev: It didn’t, actually.
qs.x: Asked whether the penalty stopped him, Hollis admits it did not. He suspected the student wanted to see friends’ work, but no copying is confirmed.

qs.q: What is the purpose of the form in Josefina’s grace period?
o: To give the teacher written proof to show parents
To decide which students should receive a penalty
To replace the need for any final deadline at all
To show her who needs help organizing their work
qs.ev: the form tells me which kids need help with planning
qs.x: The form reveals which students need help with planning. The grace period has no penalty, and Josefina adds a final deadline separately.

qs.q: Why does Hollis agree to the proposal?
o: The maximum penalty would be twenty percent.
A firm cut-off would prevent students from abusing it.
Farah agrees to a five percent daily penalty.
Students with plans would be exempt from it.
qs.ev: A real final deadline. I could live with that.
qs.x: He objects to the twenty percent cap until Josefina adds the unit-test cut-off, then accepts. The cap alone made him worry about gaming.

qs.q: What condition does Farah attach to accepting a penalty?
o: The pilot must last for a full school year.
The penalty must stop after forty-eight hours.
Students with formal accommodations must be excluded.
Every student must complete a planning form.
qs.ev: if students with an accommodation plan are exempt
qs.x: She accepts five percent a day only if students with accommodation plans are exempt. She asks for a one-term pilot, not a full year.

qs.q: How will the teachers decide whether the policy works?
o: They will review the results after one term.
They will let the principal make the final decision.
They will survey parents at the end of the year.
They will compare their marks with other schools.
qs.ev: One term, and then we look at the data.
qs.x: They agree to a one-term pilot and then look at late-submission data. The principal receives the written policy but is not asked to judge it.

parts.context: You will hear a report about a proposal to pay grandparents who provide child care.

lines: In many families, the most trusted child care provider isn’t a centre or a nanny. It’s Grandma. Now the province is considering whether grandparents who provide regular care should be paid for it. Under a proposal released for public comment this week, grandparents who look after a grandchild under four for at least twenty hours a week could receive a monthly benefit of four hundred dollars. Supporters say the idea simply recognizes work that is already being done. They point out that a licensed space can cost the province far more than that per child, and that, in rural areas and for parents working night shifts, licensed care often isn’t available at all. Some also argue that grandparents provide a continuity that no centre can match: the same caregiver, the same language and the same traditions every day. Critics, however, see two problems. Early childhood educators argue that licensed programs offer something families can’t easily replicate at home, including trained staff, structured play and early screening for developmental delays. They worry that a payment, even a modest one, could encourage families to choose grandparent care for financial reasons, even when a child would benefit from a group setting. Others raise a different concern: the burden on grandparents themselves. Rosalind Achterberg looks after her two granddaughters four days a week.

I love them to pieces, and I wouldn’t trade it. But I’m sixty-eight, and by Thursday afternoon I’m exhausted. Would four hundred dollars be nice? Of course. But I worry that once it’s a paid arrangement, it becomes much harder to tell my daughter I need a break, or that I’m not well enough this week. Right now it’s a gift. I don’t want it to become a job I can’t quit.

Researchers who study aging note that the care often falls on grandmothers, many of whom retired early or cut back their hours to provide it, sometimes at the expense of their own pensions. Some suggest the money would be better spent on respite programs, or on drop-in centres where grandparents and children can attend together, combining family care with some of the benefits of a group setting. The province says no decision will be made until the consultation closes in March, and that it is also studying whether recipients should be required to complete a basic first-aid course. Officials have also not said whether the benefit would be taxable, or whether it would affect seniors’ other government payments, two questions that grandparents’ groups say must be answered before anyone signs up. Several of those groups are holding information sessions at libraries and community centres over the winter, so that older residents can understand the proposal and submit their own comments before the deadline.

qs.q: Who would be eligible for the proposed benefit?
o: Any grandparent who lives in the same home as a young child
Grandparents caring for a child under four at least twenty hours weekly
Parents in rural areas who work night shifts and lack licensed care
Grandparents who have completed an approved first-aid course
qs.ev: who look after a grandchild under four for at least twenty hours a week
qs.x: The benefit requires caring for a grandchild under four for twenty or more hours a week. A first-aid course is only being studied as a possible future requirement.

qs.q: According to supporters, what is one advantage of grandparent care?
o: It offers early screening for developmental delays.
It costs families less than hiring a nanny.
It provides structured play every single day.
It gives children consistency in language and routine.
qs.ev: the same caregiver, the same language and the same traditions every day
qs.x: Supporters stress continuity of caregiver, language and traditions. Screening and structured play are what educators say licensed programs offer.

qs.q: What concern do early childhood educators raise?
o: Grandparents will soon demand higher payments.
Licensed centres will lose their government funding.
Money might lead families to choose against the child’s needs.
Grandparents lack the energy to care for toddlers.
qs.ev: could encourage families to choose grandparent care for financial reasons

p1.text:
Dear Ms. Beaulieu,

I hope you don’t mind me reaching out directly rather than waiting for parent-teacher interviews in November. I have taught Mathis since September, and I want to share some observations while there is still plenty of time to act on them.

Let me start with the positives, because there are many. Mathis is one of the kindest students in my class. When a new student arrived from overseas last month, he was the first to invite her to join his group, and he has been quietly helping her follow instructions using a translation app on the class tablet. He also has a real gift for drawing; his comic-strip book report was the best in the class.

That said, I have noticed a change over the past four weeks. Mathis used to participate eagerly in discussions, but he now rarely raises his hand. He has missed three math homework assignments and seems tired in the mornings, sometimes resting his head on his desk during first period. On Tuesday, when I asked whether everything was all right, he shrugged and said he was “just bored.” I’m not convinced that’s the whole story.

I want to be clear that I am not writing because Mathis is in trouble. His marks are still at grade level, although his math mark has dropped from a B+ to a C. I am writing because changes like these sometimes have causes outside school, and you know him far better than I do.

Would you be available for a short phone call or meeting next week? I’m free most days after 3:30, and I could also do an early morning before classes if that’s easier with your work schedule. If you think it would help, I could ask our school counsellor, Ms. Adebayo, to join us, but I’m happy to start with just the two of us.

In the meantime, I’ll keep an eye on him and make sure he knows my door is always open.

Warm regards,
Ignatius Rowe

p3.title: The Case for Doing Nothing: Why Children Need Boredom
paras: Ask a group of Canadian parents to describe a typical week for their school-aged children, and many will recite a schedule that would exhaust an adult: swimming on Monday, piano on Tuesday, coding club on Wednesday, hockey practice twice a week and a tournament most weekends. A national survey of parents last year found that children aged six to twelve spent an average of nine hours a week in organized activities, nearly double the figure reported two decades earlier. When asked why, parents most often said they wanted their children to discover their talents. But many also admitted to a less comfortable motive: a fear that if their child sat at home while classmates were busy, the child would fall behind. Free time, in this view, is time wasted.

A growing body of research suggests the opposite may be true. In one widely cited experiment, adults who first completed a deliberately dull task, copying numbers from a phone directory, then came up with more inventive uses for a pair of plastic cups than adults who skipped the boring step. Psychologists believe that when the mind is under-stimulated, it begins to wander, and that this wandering allows ideas to connect in unexpected ways. For children, the effect may be even stronger. Teachers frequently report that the stories, inventions and games children bring to school were dreamed up on a rainy afternoon with nothing to do. As one researcher put it, boredom is not the absence of thinking but an invitation to think differently.

Unstructured play offers benefits that organized activities rarely provide. When children make up a game in a backyard, they must agree on the rules, settle disputes and decide what to do when someone feels left out, all without an adult referee. These are precisely the negotiation and problem-solving skills that employers now say young workers lack. Children at free play also take small, manageable risks, such as climbing a little higher or exploring a ravine, which helps them learn to judge danger for themselves. Despite this, time for free play has been shrinking even at school; in several provinces, recess has been shortened to make room for additional instruction, a trend that many pediatricians have publicly criticized, warning that children who sit for most of the school day also find it harder to concentrate.

None of this means parents should cancel every activity or leave children alone for hours. Experts are careful to distinguish healthy boredom from neglect, and they acknowledge that children in crowded apartments or unsafe neighbourhoods may have few places to play freely. The bigger obstacle for most families, however, is the screen. A tablet can fill every idle moment instantly, so the uncomfortable stretch in which creativity begins never arrives. Some families have had success with simple rules, such as no devices on weekend mornings, or a “boredom jar” filled with ideas that children can draw from only after they have tried to entertain themselves for twenty minutes. The goal, one psychologist explained, is not to eliminate structure, but to leave enough empty space for children to fill on their own.

p4.title: It’s Time to End the Tutoring Arms Race
p4.byline: Opinion | by Priscilla Nakamura-Wolfe, parent and school trustee
p4.text:
When my daughter was in Grade 4, a classmate’s mother asked me, in the school parking lot, which math tutor we used. When I said we didn’t have one, she looked at me with genuine concern. “You’re brave,” she said. I have thought about that word ever since. In some Canadian neighbourhoods, sending a child to school without private tutoring now seems not just unusual but reckless.

The numbers bear this out. Tutoring companies have multiplied over the past fifteen years, and many now market themselves to parents of children as young as four. Surveys suggest that roughly one in three families in large cities pays for some form of private academic help, and in some communities the share is far higher. Families routinely spend several thousand dollars a year, and the most sought-after tutors have waiting lists.

I want to be fair to parents. Each family that hires a tutor is making a reasonable decision. If everyone else’s child is getting extra help, no one wants their own child to be the one left behind. But that is precisely what makes this an arms race: what is rational for each family is harmful for all of us together. When most children in a class are tutored, the bar for what counts as “ahead” simply rises, and families must pay even more just to stay in the same place.

The harm falls hardest on families who cannot pay. A child whose parents work two jobs, or who are new to the country, competes for scholarships and program spots against children who have had years of one-on-one coaching. Our public schools were meant to give every child an equal starting line. Private tutoring quietly moves that line back for some and forward for others.

There is a subtler cost, too. Widespread tutoring hides problems in the classroom. If a teacher’s fractions unit is confusing, but half the class has a tutor who explains it again on Thursday evening, the weakness never shows up in test results. Schools receive the wrong signal, and the students without tutors bear the consequences alone.

And then there are the children themselves. I have met eleven-year-olds whose week includes school, two tutoring sessions, music lessons and sports, with homework squeezed in after nine p.m. We should not be surprised when they tell us they are anxious.

I am not arguing that tutoring should be banned, or that it never helps. For a child with a learning disability, specialized support can be life-changing, and it should be far more available than it is. My argument is that extra help should be a public service, not a private purchase.

Concretely, I propose that every school board fund free after-school homework help in every school, staffed by teachers and trained senior students who earn volunteer hours or a modest wage. Several boards have tried this on a small scale, and attendance has been strong wherever it is offered close to home and in the early evening. Boards should also collect and publish data on which units students find hardest, so that teaching, not tutoring, improves.

Parents can help, too, by talking openly with each other. The arms race depends on everyone assuming that everyone else is buying. Sometimes the bravest thing a parent can do is say, out loud, “We don’t have a tutor, and that’s okay.”

t2.intro: A local high school is reviewing its policy on what students wear and has asked parents and community members for their input.
t2.question: Which option do you prefer?
t2.a: Require a simple school uniform (a polo shirt and dark pants, shorts or a skirt), available at several stores for a total cost of about $150 per year.
t2.b: Keep a dress code only: students choose their own clothing, but certain items, such as clothing with offensive messages, are not allowed.
t2.model:
Although I can see the advantages of uniforms, I prefer Option B, keeping a dress code.

My main reason is that teenagers learn a great deal by making their own choices. High school is a time when young people are figuring out who they are, and clothing is one of the safest ways for them to express that. A dress code still sets clear limits, such as banning offensive messages, so students learn that freedom comes with responsibility, which is an important lesson before they enter the workplace.

Second, I am not convinced that uniforms would save families money. At $150 a year, they seem affordable, but students would still need everyday clothes for evenings and weekends. For families with several children, that is an additional cost rather than a replacement.

Supporters argue that uniforms reduce bullying over expensive brands, and that is a fair concern. However, students usually find other ways to show status, such as phones, shoes or backpacks, so I doubt the effect would be large.

Overall, a clear dress code respects students while keeping the school environment appropriate.

t1.prompt: Your cousin has been accepted to two universities. One is close to home and much cheaper, and she could live with her parents. The other is in another province, has a better reputation in her field and offers a small scholarship, but she would have to move away and take out a large loan. Advise your cousin on how to decide.
t1.model: Congratulations first of all, because getting into both is a big deal. I think you need to look at this from three angles. The first is money, and I mean real numbers. Sit down with your parents and work out exactly how much the loan would be after the scholarship, and what your monthly payments would look like after graduation. A lot of people say “it’s an investment,” but if you’re paying four hundred dollars a month for ten years, that’s going to affect where you can live and what jobs you can accept. Second, I’d find out whether the reputation difference really matters in your field. Email a couple of professionals in the industry, or check LinkedIn to see where people in jobs you admire studied. Sometimes the local program is just as respected by employers. Third, think about what kind of person you are. Some people really grow when they move away and have to be independent, while others get homesick and struggle. If you’ve never lived away from home, maybe you could visit the other campus for a weekend first. Whatever you choose, remember that you could also start locally and transfer later. It doesn’t have to be a forever decision.

t2.prompt: Talk about a time when you shared a home with relatives or other family members. What was the experience like?
t2.model: When I was fourteen, my grandparents came from Lebanon and lived with us for almost two years while they waited for their own apartment. We had a small three-bedroom house, so I had to give up my room and share with my younger brother, and honestly, I was pretty resentful at first. The house was suddenly crowded and loud, and my grandmother had very strong opinions about everything, from my clothes to what time I went to bed. But over time, it became one of my favourite periods. My grandfather taught me to play backgammon, and we played every single evening after dinner. My grandmother taught me to cook her stuffed grape leaves, which I still make today. Looking back, I realize how lucky I was. I learned so much about my family’s history that I would never have known otherwise.

t3.prompt: Describe some things that are happening in the picture as well as you can. The person you are speaking to cannot see the picture.
t3.model: This picture shows a school sports day in a park on a bright, sunny day. Across the top, there’s a big green banner that says “Sports Day.” On the left side, two kids, a boy in a red shirt and a girl in a blue shirt, are racing each other between some orange cones, and they’re running as fast as they can. A teacher in a white shirt is standing nearby, pointing and cheering them on. In the middle, there’s a white tent over a table with cups of water, and a woman in a purple shirt is handing a drink to a boy who looks thirsty. On the right, a dad in a grey shirt is taking photos, and a girl in a yellow T-shirt is standing with a soccer ball at her feet, probably waiting for her event.

t4.prompt: In this picture, what do you think will most probably happen next?
t4.model: I think the race is almost over, and the girl in the blue shirt looks like she’s about to pass the boy in red, so she’ll probably win by a few steps. The teacher will run over to congratulate them both and maybe write down the result on a clipboard. After that, both runners will head straight to the water tent, because they’ll be hot and out of breath, and the woman will hand them each a cup. Meanwhile, the girl with the soccer ball is clearly waiting for her turn, so I expect the next event will be a soccer game or a penalty-kick contest. The dad with the camera will probably move closer to the field to get a good shot of his child. Later in the afternoon, I imagine there’ll be a ceremony with ribbons for the winners.

t5.intro: Your family is choosing one activity for your eight-year-old son this year. Choose the option that you prefer. In the next section, you will need to persuade a family member that your choice is better than the one they prefer.

other.title: Minor hockey
details: $750 for the season, plus about $400 for equipment
Three times a week, including 6 a.m. practices

t5.persuade: Your partner prefers minor hockey. Persuade your partner that your choice is better.
t5.model: I know you loved hockey as a kid, and I agree the team spirit is great. But I really think swimming is the better choice this year. First, think about our schedule. Hockey is three times a week, with six a.m. practices and travel tournaments on weekends. With both of us working full-time and our daughter’s dance classes, that would take over our whole family life. Swimming is just one Saturday morning. Second, the cost. Hockey would be over eleven hundred dollars with equipment, while ten weeks of swimming is only one sixty. And most importantly, swimming is a safety skill. We spend every summer at your parents’ cottage on the lake, and he still can’t swim properly. That honestly worries me. Let’s get him confident in the water this year, and if he’s still keen, we can look at hockey next fall.

t6.situation: Your neighbour’s seventeen-year-old son tutors your ten-year-old daughter in math twice a week, and you pay him $25 an hour. Your daughter says he spends much of each session on his phone, and her math marks have not improved. His mother is a close friend who arranged this so he could save money for college.
options: Talk to the tutor and explain what needs to change.
Talk to his mother and explain why you want to end the tutoring.
t6.note: Choose ONE option and speak to that person.
t6.model: Hey, Owen, do you have a minute before you start with Mia today? First, I want to say she really likes you, and I appreciate you making time for her with everything you’ve got going on in Grade Twelve. But I have to be honest about something. Mia mentioned that you’re on your phone quite a bit during the sessions, and her marks haven’t gone up since we started in September. Since I’m paying for an hour, I need the full hour to be about math. So here’s what I’d like to try. Could you put your phone in the kitchen while you’re working with her? And could you send me a quick text after each session about what you covered? Let’s give it a month. If her next test improves, that’s great. I’d really like this to work, for both of you.

t7.prompt: Answer the following question: Should high school students be required to complete volunteer hours in order to graduate? Explain your reasons.
t7.model: I believe that high school students should be required to complete volunteer hours to graduate, as long as the requirement is reasonable and flexible. My first reason is that volunteering exposes teenagers to parts of their community they might never see otherwise. When I was in Grade Ten, I completed my hours at a seniors’ residence, mostly because it was close to my house. I ended up loving it, and I still visit a woman I met there. Without the requirement, I honestly would never have walked through those doors. Second, volunteering helps students explore careers. A teenager who thinks they want to be a vet can volunteer at an animal shelter and find out whether they actually enjoy the work. It also gives them real experience to put on their first résumé, which is very helpful when they apply for part-time jobs. Some people argue that forcing students to volunteer defeats the purpose, because volunteering should be voluntary. I understand that point, but we also require students to take physical education, and nobody says exercise should be optional. The key is flexibility. Students who work part-time or care for siblings should be able to complete their hours over the summer or count helping at a family business.

scene.alt: A grassy park with trees where an enormous red boat, as big as a house, sits on the grass far from any water. Several small children sit inside the boat looking out over the side, and a teacher in a green shirt stands on the grass in front of it pointing to a small whiteboard on an easel. Two more children with backpacks are walking toward the boat holding hands. There is a sun, a cloud, a pine tree and a bush.

t8.prompt: You and your partner are choosing a kindergarten for your five-year-old daughter. You visited an outdoor “nature kindergarten” that uses this unusual classroom. Call your partner, describe what you saw, and explain whether you think it is a good choice for your daughter. Your partner cannot see the picture.
t8.model: So I just got back from the nature kindergarten, and you will not believe their classroom. It’s a giant red boat, about the size of a house, just sitting in the middle of a grassy field with no water anywhere. The kids sit inside it and look out over the side, like they’re sailing somewhere. When I arrived, the teacher was standing in front of it with a little whiteboard on an easel, teaching them about the trees around them. Two more kids were walking up holding hands with their backpacks on. Honestly, I think Ava would love it. She’s happiest outdoors, and it’s so creative. My only worry is winter. I asked, and they said they move inside when it’s below minus fifteen, but I’d want to see that space before we decide.
